newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS -Short sterling vol set on downward path.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS -Short sterling vol set on downward path.

text.p: Short sterling options' volatility slid on Wednesday, and traders said it could still have further to go before being supported by the proximity of the British election.
The low levels seen in other short-dated contracts such as Euromarks and Eurodollars are unlikely to be reached until after a new government has been formed, they said.

"The election is passe as far as short sterling is concerned, but it needs the concrete event to allow vol to go lower," said Ian Aubrey, head of futures and options sales at Yamaichi International in London.
Traders said there has been only limited activity in LIFFE's short sterling options -- further depressing volatility.

According to LIFFE statistics, short sterling options traded only 201,221 contracts in March, down from 264,007 in February and also down from the same period a year ago when 203,169 contracts traded in March.
"No-one wants to be a buyer of vol, even though it is cheap," said a trader at a French brokerage in London. "It could go even lower. In all the short end markets, volatility is offered."
June at-the-money volatility was at 10.5-10.75 percent down from 10.8 percent on Tuesday. September was down 0.10 at 11.15 percent, and December was down slightly at 13.0-13.5 percent.
June short sterling futures were up one basis point at 93.31 by 1530 GMT, while September was up 0.03 at 93.02 and December was up 0.04 at 92.78.

Aubrey said he advised putting bullish strategies in place, as the short sterling strip was pricing in too large a rise in interest rates. December short sterling futures imply interest rates of about 7.25 percent at the end of the year -- well above the current base rate level of 6.0 percent.
"We're saying buy December 93.00 calls and sell the 92.25 puts," he said. "You don't need to hold it to expiration, but I can't see rates more than 6.5 to 6.75 percent."

Traders said there was interest in the opinion polls ahead of the May 1 election, with the opposition Labour Party's current lead of 14 percentage points regarded as sealing the Conservative government's fate.
In contrast to the 1992 election, there appeared to be little sign of investor worries about the prospect of a Labour government.
"The only real shock for the market would be the Tories winning," said Aubrey.
